title: The Immune System
objective: After this level you can explain how white blood cells fight infection.
summary: Innate immunity includes skin and phagocytes, found by Metchnikoff in 1882. Acquired immunity uses B cells that make antibodies, T cells, and memory.

cards.headline: In 1882, a zoologist stuck splinters into see-through starfish larvae.
cards.body: Elie Metchnikoff was studying the tiny animals in Messina, Italy. What he saw crowding around those splinters became one of the first clues to how your own body fights infection.

cards.headline: The devouring cells
cards.body: Certain cells in the larvae surrounded the splinters and engulfed them. Metchnikoff named them phagocytes, from Greek words meaning 'devouring cells', and the discovery earned him a share of the 1908 Nobel Prize. You have phagocytes too: white blood cells that swallow germs and dead or damaged cells. Your body runs its own cleanup crew, and it eats on the job.

cards.headline: The defenses you were born with
cards.body: Phagocytes belong to your innate immunity, the defense system you're born with. It's nonspecific: it doesn't need to know which germ it's facing. It also includes barriers like the skin from Level 71, which keeps harmful material out in the first place. Think of a wall with guards who throw out anything that doesn't belong.

cards.headline: Specialists who learn and remember
cards.body: Your second defense, acquired immunity, develops as you meet germs. It relies on lymphocytes, white blood cells of two kinds. B cells become plasma cells that make antibodies: proteins that lock onto one specific antigen, usually a protein on a germ's surface, and make it easier to destroy. T cells attack directly and help run the response. Afterwards, some B and T cells stay on as memory, so the next time that germ turns up, the answer comes faster.

mascot.line: Hold on to memory cells. Vaccines, two levels on, are built on them.

cards.headline: Immune system: met
learned: Phagocytes are white blood cells that engulf germs
Innate immunity, including skin, is the defense you are born with
B cells make antibodies that fit one specific antigen
Memory cells make the second response faster

questions.prompt: What did Metchnikoff see certain cells do to the splinters in starfish larvae?

options.label: Push them out through the skin
options.rationale: The cells came to the splinters and engulfed them.

options.label: Dissolve them with acid
options.rationale: The cells engulfed the splinters; that's what 'phagocyte' means.

options.label: Make antibodies against them
options.rationale: Antibodies come from B cells, part of acquired immunity.

questions.explanation: Metchnikoff saw cells surround and engulf the splinters, and named them phagocytes, 'devouring cells'.

questions.prompt: Why does acquired immunity respond faster the second time the same germ shows up?

options.label: The germ is weaker the second time
options.rationale: It's the same germ; your defenses are what changed.

options.label: Your skin grows thicker after an infection
options.rationale: The speed-up comes from memory cells, not skin.

options.label: Some B and T cells stay on as memory
Phagocytes learn to recognize every germ
options.rationale: Phagocytes are nonspecific; memory belongs to lymphocytes.

questions.explanation: After an infection, some B and T cells remain as memory, so the response to the same antigen is faster next time.

questions.prompt: From Level 12: phagocytes and lymphocytes are both white blood cells. Where in your body are they made?

options.label: In the yellow marrow of long bones
options.rationale: Yellow marrow is mostly fat, an energy store.

options.label: In the red marrow inside some bones
In the skin's tough outer layer
options.rationale: That layer is dead keratin-packed cells, a wall.

options.label: In the liver, alongside the bile
options.rationale: The liver makes bile; red marrow makes blood cells.

questions.explanation: Phagocytes and lymphocytes are white blood cells, and red marrow in the spaces of spongy bone makes your blood cells.
